title: Sodom didn’t fall overnight—it rotted in plain sight.
paragraphs: Sodom didn’t fall overnight—it rotted in plain sight.

At first, it didn’t look like rebellion.
It looked like prosperity.

Full tables.
Secure walls.
Busy markets.
Everything appeared blessed.
But beneath the surface, something darker was growing.
Scripture pulls back the curtain in Ezekiel 16:49:
“She had pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy.”
Did you catch that?

Not fire.
Not judgment.
Not destruction.
Pride came first.

Then comfort.
Then indifference.
And indifference is where decay finds a home.
Sin rarely storms the front door.
It seeps through the cracks.

A compromise here.
A silence there.
A truth ignored because it’s inconvenient.
And slowly…

What once shocked you
no longer moves you.
By the time we reach Genesis 19, Sodom isn’t just sinful—it’s normalized sin.

What was once hidden became public.
What was once resisted became celebrated.
What was once shameful became identity.
That’s the danger.

Not just sin…
but sin that no longer feels like sin.
And here’s where it gets personal:

Sodom is not just a city.
It’s a warning pattern.

Because the same progression can happen in a culture…
a church…
a family…
or a single heart.
God didn’t ignore Sodom.
He warned it.

Through Abraham’s intercession.
Through Lot’s presence.
Grace was extended before judgment ever fell.
Because God is not eager to destroy.
He is patient.
But patience is not permission.
And when repentance never comes…
Justice eventually does.
Fire didn’t start the story.
It finished it.
But here’s the part many miss:
The story of Sodom is not just about destruction.
It’s about escape.
Lot was pulled out.
Why?

Not because he was perfect.
But because God still rescues those who respond.
That’s the Gospel pattern.
Not perfection → salvation.
But sin → conviction → repentance → grace → redemption.
And that redemption has a name:
Jesus Christ.

Where Sodom faced fire,
Jesus stepped into it.

Where judgment was deserved,
He took it on the cross.
So that no one has to end where Sodom ended.

If you feel the drift…
If conviction is still alive in you…
That’s not condemnation.
That’s mercy calling you back.

Reflection:
Where have you slowly become comfortable with what God once warned you about?
This isn’t the end of your story.
